original_question: Can one prove the fundamental theorems of fractional calculus for exact fractional differences of non-integer order that arise in lattice fractional calculus and exact-difference approaches to nonlocal continuum and lattice mechanics?
target_in_paper: Section 4.1, "Nonlocal continuum and lattice mechanics": the unnumbered open problem stated at the end of the discussion of lattice fractional calculus/exact differences, namely that for the exact fractional differences proposed in the cited lattice-fractional-calculus papers, the fundamental theorems of fractional calculus have not been proved for non-integer orders.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the right part of the paper: exact fractional differences, the non-integer-order regime, and the lattice-fractional-calculus / nonlocal continuum-and-lattice-mechanics context. It also correctly frames the task as a proof problem about the fundamental theorems of fractional calculus, which matches the paper's §4.1 open-problem wording.
missing_details: The paper's exact target is an unnumbered open problem in Section 4.1, not a numbered conjecture or theorem elsewhere in the article.

The operator class should be pinned down as the exact fractional differences introduced in the lattice-fractional-calculus / exact-discretization works cited there, namely refs. [144], [146], and [147] in the paper.

The phrase "fundamental theorems of fractional calculus" is left implicit in Section 4.1; to make the question stand-alone, it should be unpacked as the discrete analogues of the 1st and 2nd Fundamental Theorems, i.e. suitable left- and right-inverse identities between exact fractional differences and their companion exact fractional integral/summation operators.

The quantifier should be explicit: the problem concerns non-integer orders, best stated as every non-integer order α > 0 for which the exact fractional-difference operators are defined; Section 4.1 does not impose a narrower order range.

The function class must be specified: the paper does not say on which spaces of lattice functions these identities should hold, although its analytical sections consistently formulate such theorems on appropriate spaces.
It is not stated whether the intended scope is only the one-dimensional lattice case or also the n-dimensional lattice-fractional-calculus setting mentioned in Section 4.1.

If the 2nd Fundamental Theorem is intended, any discrete boundary/initial correction terms must be made explicit, since the paper's continuous formulations show that right-inverse identities may involve such terms.

No ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree restriction, nilpotency condition, or asymptotic quantifier such as "for all sufficiently large m" appears in this paper's formulation; these notions are not part of the target problem and should not be imported.
refined_question: Can one establish, for the exact fractional difference operators of every non-integer order α > 0 arising in lattice fractional calculus/exact discretization, the discrete analogues of the 1st and 2nd Fundamental Theorems of fractional calculus on suitable spaces of lattice functions; that is, the appropriate left- and right-inverse relations between those exact fractional differences and the associated exact fractional summation/integration operators, with any necessary boundary or initial correction terms stated explicitly?
justification: This is the nearest paper-faithful target because Section 4.1 explicitly singles out the lack of proofs of the fundamental theorems of fractional calculus for exact fractional differences of non-integer order in the lattice-fractional-calculus framework. To make that sentence into a sharp stand-alone research question, the paper's own earlier sections must be used to unpack what the "fundamental theorems of FC" mean: Section 2.1 gives the left-inverse desideratum, Section 2.2 formulates the 1st Fundamental Theorem as relation (11), and Section 2.3 states both 1st- and 2nd-theorem identities for general FC operators. I therefore kept the question narrowly on exact fractional differences and did not broaden it to neighboring issues in Section 4.1 such as fractional vector calculus, continuum limits, or quantum-field applications.
